name: Papua New Guinea
summary: The eastern half of New Guinea, ruled by Britain, Germany and then Australia, independent in 1975; over 800 languages are spoken.

knownFor.label: Sing-sing
knownFor.note: Highland gatherings with dance and costumes.

location.value: Eastern New Guinea and islands; about 463,000 km².

terrain.value: A mountainous mainland and hundreds of islands, with 14 active volcanoes and vast rainforests.

resources.value: Minerals such as gold and copper, oil and natural gas.

population.value: Officially about 11.8 million, though satellite estimates suggest closer to 17 million.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural: only 14% lived in towns in 2023.

disease.value: Poorly developed health care; high HIV/AIDS rates and outbreaks of cholera and tuberculosis.

migration.value: Most people live in rural areas (about 86%, 2023); people move to towns for work.

economicBase.value: Resource extraction (28% of GDP in 2018): minerals, oil and gas; farming employs the most people.

tradeRoutes.value: There are 22 international ports, but only two of five highways reach the interior.

inequality.value: Poverty is most common in rural areas, where services are harder to reach. Gini index 41.9 (2009).

governmentType.value: A Commonwealth realm with a Westminster-style parliamentary system led by a prime minister.

keyRulers.value: Michael Somare, the first prime minister.

succession.value: The National Parliament elects the prime minister.

institutions.value: The unicameral National Parliament, whose members also serve as provincial leaders.

stability.value: An uprising on Bougainville from 1988 became a civil war; a peace agreement was signed in 2001.

eliteConflict.value: Parties are not ideologically different; governments are coalitions, and votes of no confidence are common (the prime minister was replaced in 2019).

armyAndTech.value: The Papua New Guinea Defence Force, which has also been used for internal security.

majorWars.value: Fierce fighting in the New Guinea campaign of World War II, including the Kokoda Track (1942); later the Bougainville conflict.

territoryChange.value: Bougainville voted 98.31% for independence in a non-binding referendum (2019).

alliancesRivals.value: Keeps close ties with Australia and good relations with Indonesia and the Solomon Islands.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy was 63.4% in 2015; churches run much of the schooling.

openness.value: Open to foreign investment, with restrictions: the Bougainville Mining Act (2015) gave customary landowners a veto over future mining. Foreign investment was deterred after 1980s law-and-order problems.

communicationTransport.value: Air travel is the most reliable transport; only two of five highways reach the interior.

religion.value: A large Christian majority; Christianity became the official state religion in March 2025.

languageWriting.value: 840 known languages, the most of any country; English and Tok Pisin are common languages, and Hiri Motu is also used.

socialStructure.value: Many small groups; the wantok system of kin networks expects mutual loyalty and benefits.

sharedIdentity.value: The idea of a "country" was foreign to many at independence; great diversity has caused political friction.

dailyLife.value: Sweet potato became the staple food in the highlands.

colonisation.value: German and British, then Australian rule (1884–1975).

declineSignals.value: Declining effectiveness: civil service politicisation and declining government services, with the lowest HDI in the Pacific (2019).

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
